1 learned Predecessor of this Tribunal, dated 15.05.2023, has been partly set aside and the matter has been remanded for reassessment only to the limited extent as to whether the insurance company is entitled to recovery rights against the Appellant / respondent no.2 (Owner of the offending vehicle)
who pleads to have exercised due care and caution in handing over the offending vehicle to respondent no.1 /driver who was found to be not holding any valid driving licence.
2.
For this purpose, respondent no.2 was granted another opportunity to lead evidence.
In order to prove his defence, respondent no.2 examined himself as R-2W-1.
He tendered his evidence by way of affidavit Ex.R2W1/A wherein he deposed that he was registered owner of the offending vehicle.
He testified that in year 2016, respondent no.1 approached him for the job of a driver.
R2W1 enquired about the period since when such driver had been driving and checked his licence.
He deposed that the licence furnished by respondent no.1 showed to be valid for heavy transport vehicles and bore sealed and signature of District Transport Office Tuensang, Nagaland.
He further deposed that he checked the credentials of respondent no.1 and ensured that his past track report was satisfactory, before employing him as his MACT No:965/18 Deepak Kumar v. Taarif & ors.

He further took his driving test and only on being satisfied with his driving skills, employed him as his driver.
He deposed that respondent no.1 worked as a driver for R2W1 for 14 months.
R2W1 relied upon Registration Certificate as Ex.R2W1/1, Goods Carrier's Permit and Certificate of Fitness as Ex.R2W1/2 and copy of driving licence of respondent no.1as Ex.R3W1/D.
He was cross-examined by learned counsel for insurance company.
3. In order to ascertained and fixed liability on the owner of an offending vehicle, breach of conditions of the insurance policy by such owner have to be proved.

It has been held by Hon'ble Supreme Court in IFFCO Tokio General Insurance Company v. Geeta Devi and Ors. (2024) 13SCC 755, held that in order to claim recovery rights, insurance company must establish infringement or violation of the conditions of the insurance policy.

entities.text: IFFCO Tokio General Insurance Company v. Geeta Devi and Ors. (2024) 13SCC 755
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It further held that such breach by the insured must be willful and fundamental.

The Court, while referring to its judgment in National Insurance Company vs. Swaran Singh (2004) 3SCC 297, observed:
"...16.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The findings summed up by the Bench, to the extent presently relevant, are as under: (Swaran Singh5, SCC pp.341-42, para 110) "110....(iii) The brach of policy condition e.g. disqualification of the driver or invalid driving licence of the driver, as contained in sub-section (2)(a)(ii) of Section 149, has to be proved to have been committed by the insured for avoiding liability by the insurer.

Mere absence, fake or invalid driving licence or disqualification of the driver for driving at the relevant time,
are not in themselves defences available to the insurer against either the insured or the third parties.

To avoid its liability towards the insured, the insurer has to prove that the insured was guilty of MACT No:965/18 Deepak Kumar v. Taarif & ors. P.No.
3 Of 6 ss negligence and failed to exercise reasonable care in the matter of fulfilling the condition of the policy regarding use of vehicles by a duly licensed driver or one who was not disqualified to drive at the relevant time.

(iv) Insurance companies, however, with a view to avoid their liability must not only establish the available defence(s) raised in the said proceedings but must also establish "breach" on the part of the owner of the vehicle; the burden of proof wherefor would be on them.
(v) The court cannot lay down any criteria as to how the said burden would be discharged, inasmuch as the same.
would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case.

(vi) Even where the insurer is able to prove breach on the part of the insured concerning the policy condition regarding holding of a valid licence by the driver or his qualification to drive during the relevant period, the insurer would not be allowed to avoid its liability towards the insured unless the said breach or breaches on the condition of driving licence is/are so fundamental as are found to have contributed to the cause of the accident.

The Tribunals in interpreting the policy conditions would apply "the rule of main purpose"
and the concept of "fundamental breach" to allow defences available to the insurer under Section 149(2) of the Act.
(vii) The question, as to whether the owner has taken reasonable care to find out as to whether the driving licence produced by the driver (a fake one or otherwise), does not fulfil the requirements of law or not will have to be determined in each case..."

In these circumstances, such an owner who did not infringe or violate the condition of the insurance policy willfully or knowingly, cannot be held accountable to a third party or liable to recovery of the compensation payable by the insurance company to such third party.

In the instant case, respondent no.2 has relied upon a copy of driving licence Ex.R2W1/B which shows it to have been valid MACT No:965/18 Deepak Kumar v. Taarif & ors. P.No. 4 Of 6 ss as on date of accident.
It is only on subsequent verification of such driving licence by the police during investigation of FIR no.809/2017 that such driving licence was found to be fake.
As per the testimony of R2W1, the owner of the offending vehicle had made every effort to check the credentials of the driver /respondent no.1 and thereby exercised due care and caution.

A plea has been raised by the insurance company that an FIR was registered under Section 3/181 of MV Act against the owner of the offending vehicle and a chargesheet was also subsequently filed against him for having permitted his vehicle to be driven by a person not holding a valid driving licence.
It is pleaded that throughout the investigation, respondent no.2 never produced or handed over the copy of driving licence of respondent no.1.

It is further pleaded that even upon issuance of notice by the insurance company under Order 12 Rule 8 CPC, respondent no.2 did not produce the fake driving licence that was allegedly handed over to him by respondent no.1.

It has been argued that failure by respondent no.2, to produce the alleged fake driving licence of respondent no.1 raises doubt and a possibility that the same may have been later on procured by respondent no.2.

P.No. 5 Of 6 ss have relied on the said fake driving licence later during the proceedings, especially where the defence had been raised at the initiation of the inquiry proceedings by way of reply/written statement.

sentences.text: The insurance company is further debarred from questioning the opportunity of leading of evidence by respondent no.2 at the stage as the same has been granted to him by Hon'ble Delhi High Court vide order dated 27.11.2024.

As such, respondent no.2 is held to be not liable to compensate the petitioner and consequently insurance company is not entitled to recovery rights from respondent no.2.
4.
